author: RichardMCNgo
text:
LLM slop is text which is grammatically correct but lacks deeper meaning.

Analogously, I call a proof math slop if it’s technically correct but the result isn’t insightful or interesting.

Many scientific papers already contain math slop, but LLMs will soon produce far more.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
I used to believe @bryan_caplan’s hypothesis that higher education is mostly about signaling.

But why don’t students find much cheaper ways to signal the same traits?

My hypothesis: higher ed is instead mostly about *committing* to the norms and values of cultural elites.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
My main concern about insiders trading on prediction markets is not that decisions will leak, but that it incentivizes corruption.

E.g. inside traders could profit more by pushing for unexpected decisions.

Such harms could plausibly outweigh all benefits of prediction markets.

quoted.text: The other day a student asked me about the prevalence of insider trading in prediction markets. I now have an answer. https://t.co/CpYLCstLw5

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Great thread. I’d even go further—I think we’re still recovering from Von Neumann’s biggest mistakes:

1. Implicitly basing game theory on causal decision theory
2. Founding utility theory on the independence axiom
3. Advocating for nuking the USSR as soon as possible

quoted.text:
One of the curious things about von Neumann was his ability to do extremely impressive technical work while seemingly missing all the big insights.

He did much work on mathematical foundations in the 20s, but completely missed the incompleteness/undefinability theorems... (1/3)

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
I’m not saying you should change your *beliefs* about possible futures, just that you should change which subset of possible futures you’re aiming to improve.

Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Hypothesis: we’ll look back on mass migration as being worse for Europe than WW2 was.

Europe recovered quickly from WW2, because each country remained high-trust and homogeneous.

But you can’t just rebuild your way out of internal ethno-religious fractures.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
My biggest concern about prediction markets is that they commoditize access to power.

In the same way that every prediction market is an assassination market, it’s also a “buying decisions” market.

But institutions work only insofar as their decisions *aren’t* for sale.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Diagnosing big problems is hard, but solving them is typically far far harder.

So even people who make very insightful diagnoses often then advocate for bad responses.

Some examples IMO:
- environmentalists on climate change
- Yudkowsky on AI risk
- Yarvin on the Cathedral

author: RichardMCNgo
text: This also applies to people. A significant number of the most brilliant people I know avoid self-coercion to an extent that sometimes appears dysfunctional or even self-destructive. But it allows them to produce wonders.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Most people float around social reality as the currents take them. Some people are nails who dig in and fight the waves.

And some of those nails have found the high ground in the psychosocial landscape. They’re the fixed points around which social reality rearranges itself.

quoted.text:
Extreme virtue is a public good because it allows groups of people to create common knowledge of an ideal they’re trying to live up to.

If you are the most courageous person on the planet you serve as a fixed point that pulls everyone upwards by your example.
